title: The Wheel of Life: A Simple Way to Work Out What Needs Attention
excerpt: Sometimes you know something in your life isn’t quite right, but you’re not sure what it is. The Wheel of Life is a simple exercise that can help you step back, look at the bigger picture and identify the areas of your life that might need a little more attention.
content:
Sometimes you can feel that something isn't quite right with your life without being able to put your finger on what it is.

You might be doing fine at work, exercising regularly and have good people around you, and still feel that something is missing. When you're busy getting on with everyday life, it can be surprisingly hard to step back and look at the bigger picture.

That's where I find the Wheel of Life useful. It's a simple exercise that gives you a snapshot of how satisfied you are with different parts of your life right now. It won't tell you what you should be doing or what a good life looks like. It just gives you a few minutes to look at your life from a slightly different angle.

## Taking a snapshot

Draw a circle and divide it into eight to ten sections, each representing an important area of your life. You might include health and fitness, relationships, family and friends, career, money, personal development, fun and hobbies, your home and environment, and your sense of purpose.

Then score each area from 1 to 10. The numbers aren't meant to be scientific. There's no formula for deciding whether your relationship is a 7 or an 8. Just ask yourself how satisfied you feel with that part of your life right now.

Plot the scores on the wheel and join them up. What you end up with is a picture of how your life currently feels to you, and that's where it starts to get interesting.

## Look at the gaps

The most useful thing the wheel shows you is usually the gaps between areas, more than any overall score.

You might discover you're really happy with your career and fitness but have given your social life a 4. Your finances might be an 8 while your personal development is a 5. You might have a great relationship but realise you've left yourself almost no time for hobbies or simply having fun.

None of that is good or bad in itself, and there's no such thing as a perfect wheel. A 5 in one area doesn't automatically mean there's a problem to fix. The point is to notice where your attention is going, and where it isn't.

I find that particularly useful. It's easy to pour time into the parts of life that are already going well, because they're familiar or because they demand your attention, while other areas get neglected without you ever deciding to neglect them. Seeing it drawn out makes that hard to miss.

## The score isn't the answer

If you give your social life a 4, going out more isn't necessarily the fix. The more useful question is why it's a 4.

Perhaps you aren't making enough effort to see friends. Maybe you've become too focused on work, or you've moved away from people you used to see regularly. Or maybe you're perfectly happy with your social life and the score is low because you're comparing it with what you think it *should* look like.

So the number matters less than what it makes you think about. Writing things down helps here. If you give an area a particularly low score, spend a few minutes explaining to yourself why. What feels missing? What would you like it to look like? Is there something you could realistically change? The problem might turn out to be different from what you first thought.

## From reflection to action

The danger with exercises like this is producing a nice-looking wheel and then forgetting about it. The useful part comes afterwards.

Rather than trying to improve everything at once, pick one or two areas you'd really like to change, and turn each into something specific:

- Instead of "improve my social life", you might decide to "arrange to see a friend at least twice a month".
- Instead of "work on my health", you might decide to "train three times a week for the next month".

You're looking for a practical next step on something that matters to you, without trying to transform an area of your life overnight. I think that's important, because personal development can easily become an endless hunt for things about yourself that need improving, and I don't find that very helpful. The wheel is there to help you notice where you are and decide whether there's somewhere you'd rather be.

## Come back to it

I think most of the value comes from doing it more than once. Do it today, then come back to it in three or six months. Some scores might have improved. Others might have stayed exactly where they were. You might even find that something which felt important a few months ago doesn't matter much to you any more, which is worth knowing too.

That's what makes the Wheel of Life interesting to me. You can't pass or fail it, and it doesn't measure how successful your life is. It's a way of stopping for a moment to ask a question most of us don't ask often enough: how happy am I with the life I'm actually living, and what could I do to make it a little better?
